content_summary.framing: Miller opens: LVT is 'a tax we don't currently have in the UK, but one that has something of a cult following' [0:31]. Stated aims: what an LVT is, when and why one might want it, whether it can be done in practice, other ways of taxing land. There is no revenue-neutral rate, no land-share estimate, no council tax or stamp duty revenue figure anywhere in the episode.
content_summary.how_it_works: [1:42-5:00] An annual tax on land value distinct from buildings. Efficient because land is fixed in supply, cannot move, and the bill is the same whoever owns it or whatever is built: no substitution effect, only an income effect (Adam/Zaranko). Wrinkle [6:31-8:00]: land value depends on permitted use, so an LVT based on market value can distort incentives to seek planning permission; definitions (market value, best-use value, stripped of 'hope value') differ in how much they do this. Different from a tax on uplift [38:30-40:30].
content_summary.who_gains_loses_and_capitalisation: [9:00-11:30] Whoever owns land when the tax is announced loses the capitalised value of the whole future tax stream whether they keep paying or sell; a later buyer pays a correspondingly lower price and is 'no worse off'. Participants call it 'basically a one-off wealth tax... a one-off windfall tax on people who own land at that point in time' (quote Q2). They add: it hits people at peak wealth (around retirement), those who chose to hold wealth as land rather than spend it or hold it as pension/cash, and includes ordinary freehold houses, not just estates [12:00-14:30]. Efficient is 'not the same thing as saying that they are good': the fairness question is a political judgement about a one-off wealth tax on land-held wealth [11:00, 51:31]. This is a statement of standard capitalisation theory; the episode cites no empirical study.
content_summary.valuation_feasibility: [22:00-30:30] Adam: separating land from buildings is 'the biggest challenge', because land is rarely sold bare in the valuable locations; experts give 'starkly contrasting views' and the truth is 'somewhere in between'. They cite, without naming a paper, the Welsh Government's commissioned studies (Valuation Office Agency, academics, consultancies): relative land values across locations can be estimated fairly reliably from comparable sales, but the land/building split needed 'some very broad brush sweeping assumptions'; 'not impossible' but 'a challenge' [24:00-25:30]. KEY CLAIM: valuation accuracy does not matter for efficiency (even a random per-plot charge is non-distortionary, because the plot's price adjusts and the owner cannot change the bill) but matters for fairness, legitimacy and appeals backlogs [25:30-30:30]. This is the IFS's own position and directly sharpens the wiki's land-cannot-be-assessed page. Not a figure they cite from others: the Welsh studies are named only generically (check against research/welsh-lvt-valuation-testing.md).
content_summary.asset_rich_cash_poor: [31:00-34:00] A reasonable worry but not specific to LVT (council tax has the same problem). Remedies: deferral until sale or death, with interest charged (a high rate if deferral should be a last resort), or a fixed deferral period; risk that people defer in hope a later government repeals the tax, so political durability matters. Matches the wiki's lvt-hurts-asset-rich-cash-poor page and the Resolution Foundation deferral design.
content_summary.replace_council_tax_stamp_duty_business_: SINGLE TAX [34:00-36:00]: Adam does 'not find it plausible'; doubts a 100% LVT could raise enough ('the numbers add up' is questioned, no figure given) and says fairness bites harder at near-100% taxation of existing wealth. BUSINESS RATES [36:00-38:00]: 'we've argued that certainly for business rates' that taxing land without buildings would be more efficient (quote Q5), and a revenue-neutral swap makes windfalls less pointed than a net new tax, though there would still be winners and losers (Oxford Street land-heavy vs. a warehouse building-heavy). COUNCIL TAX [38:00]: 'a bit different because actually we think there, we do want to tax the buildings' [ASR 'Count tax'] and listeners are referred to an earlier episode. STAMP DUTY: NOT DISCUSSED in this episode (the blurb's mention is the only reference). So the scanner's 'could it replace council tax and stamp duty' is answered only as: IFS wants council tax reformed on land-plus-buildings value (consistent with Mirrlees Housing Services Tax and the IFS's long-standing stamp-duty abolition line), not replaced by a pure LVT.
content_summary.uplift_taxes_and_section_106: [38:30-45:00] Adam: a stronger fairness case exists for taxing the uplift (infrastructure, planning permission) than for taxing the stock, because a current owner has paid market price for past uplift. But a stand-alone uplift tax invites owners to delay development hoping for repeal; an annual LVT does not, since abolition relieves the future bill. UK has partial instruments: Community Infrastructure Levy ('less than a billion pounds a year', per the speakers), section 106 agreements ('about five billion a year or so'), and the Crossrail business rate supplement. Adam on s.106: 'we don't really want taxes to be negotiated on a case by case basis... costly and uncertain and unsatisfactory' (Q7). CIL and s.106 totals are spoken approximations; use an official source (MHCLG developer contributions monitoring) if the figures are wanted.
content_summary.why_not_adopted_and_conclusions: [44:30-52:30] Participants' explanations: the UK already taxes property unusually heavily (IFS point, no OECD figure cited here; the wiki's united-kingdom page already carries 2.8% of GDP), existing council tax and business rates, losers 'always unhappy and the winners never grateful', valuation disputes. Places with LVTs mostly levy them at 'very low' rates; Estonia is called the purest case, exempting homeowners until this year then moving to a discount that still removes most homeowners (a spoken claim to verify against Estonian law); Denmark and subnational US/Australia/NZ taxes mentioned; Welsh Government groundwork and Mark Drakeford's interest noted; Burnham's 'proportional property tax' is distinguished from an LVT because it taxes land plus building [49:30]. Closing positions: Adam would 'absolutely' replace business rates with an LVT 'if you can iron out the practicalities' but doubts it is a top priority; Zaranko is 'not necessarily convinced it's worth the faff' and expects big carve-outs (homeowners, farmers, Church of England). Miller's summary: 'efficient ways to raise revenue. That is not the same thing as saying that they are good' (Q12).
content_summary.figures_and_who_owns_them: No figures originate with the authors beyond the spoken CIL/s.106 approximations. Third-party items only referenced: Mirrlees Review 2011 ('the Bible of tax design', argued for an LVT at least for businesses) [44:30]; Churchill's landlord passage and Henry George [16:30-18:00]; 1909 People's Budget 'legislated but never happened' [47:30]; Welsh Government studies; Estonia/Denmark. The episode does NOT mention the Resolution Foundation 'Home economics' report (24 Sept, i.e. after recording), Muellbauer, Tax Policy Associates/Neidle, PolicyEngine, or any revenue-neutral rate.

claim_grade: Central thesis (Vancouver treats uplift as a problem and density as a harm to neighbourhood character; the city ought to upzone more and capture more): D-claim (interpretive/argumentative), Tier 2 per people-tiers.json (independent economist-blogger; origin/proponent only, never support, never in a lead). content_summary.thesis: Value capture means the city trades extra development rights for public amenities; done well it is a win-win (more housing plus amenities). Wiebe argues Vancouver 'treats land value uplift as a problem, and use[s] value capture as a way to prevent it', and that this is explained by treating density as a harm to neighbourhood character, in which case value capture becomes a win-lose trade-off. He asks the city to be 'honest about the choices being made'.

his_examples_and_the_primary_status_of_e.wiebe_says: In 2011 the Vancouver Symphony Orchestra got a music school paid for by a housing developer, which the city allowed to build a larger apartment building with the school in the lower floors.
his_examples_and_the_primary_status_of_e.verified: Broadly true but incomplete. VSO School of Music, 843 Seymour St, opened May 2011 on the former Capitol 6 cinema site, occupying the lower floors of a residential tower; the school's own site says it was 'made possible through the City of Vancouver's Cultural Amenity Bonus Program' (vsoschoolofmusic.ca/about, org's own account). Georgia Straight (27 May 2011, Jessica Werb, journalism) reports a $30M, 25,000 sq ft facility, that Macdonald Development Corporation 'in 2005 received the largest cultural-amenity density bonus in the city's history', and that it was 'financed through the density transfer, as well as support from the provincial and federal governments, in addition to private donations' (including a $365,705 Cultural Spaces Canada grant). So the bonus was granted in 2005 and the building opened in 2011; and 'a developer paid for it' omits the public and philanthropic funding.
his_examples_and_the_primary_status_of_e.tier1_primary_needed: City of Vancouver Council report granting the Capitol 6 rezoning/cultural amenity bonus (c. 2004-05; the search tool surfaced council.vancouver.ca/20050721/documents/pe2.pdf but its content was not confirmed or readable) and the Cultural Amenity Bonus policy; City annual CAC and density bonus reports.

content_summary.arguments_vs_facts: FACT-CLAIMS (anchor on Tier 1): the three policy descriptions above, the existence of the fee/bonus requirement, who approved what and when. ARGUMENT (Wiebe's, D-claims): that 'higher land values should be celebrated'; that preventing uplift reveals the city sees housing as a harm; that the 600 sq ft allowance is 'stingy' and sixplexes on every lot would be better; that planners would be more honest to say they are preserving neighbourhoods. INTERPRETIVE GAP: the essay offers no evidence of motive beyond the city's wording of two reports. A rival reading, consistent with the City's own stated rationale, is that setting a fee ex ante limits land-price escalation and speculation so that projects remain viable (the density-bonus update is described by the City as set from economic feasibility testing 'while limiting any potential land value escalation and discouraging speculation'); the wiki's own objection page already carries evidence (Freemark 2020; Greenaway-McGrevy et al. 2021) that upzoning capitalises into land prices. The essay does not engage with this, or with Bill 46's shift away from negotiated per-project contributions. The first paragraph's illustrative $2M to $3M example is explicitly hypothetical and also appears in his earlier essay already cited on the wiki.
content_summary.recent_context_the_essay_omits: Provincial Bill 46 (Housing Statutes (Development Financing) Amendment Act, 2023; third reading 29 Nov 2023, royal assent 30 Nov 2023) added amenity cost charges (ACCs) to the Local Government Act (new Division 19.1) and the Vancouver Charter (new Part XXIV-B, ss. 523E ff.) and, in new s.565.1(2.1) of the Charter and s.482(2.1) of the LGA, provides that a zoning by-law 'must not establish conditions relating to the conservation or provision of an amenity that is specified in an amenity cost charge by-law' (text read, bclaws). Vancouver Council approved a city-wide ACC by-law on 21 July 2026 (per City release/snippet), effective 30 Sept 2026 (the day Wiebe's essay appeared): per Daily Hive (9 Jul 2026) on the staff report, rates of $2.32/sq ft at or below 1.2 FSR, $5/sq ft for 1.2-1.5 FSR and $10/sq ft above 1.5 FSR (high-density rate phased at half rate for the first year), 3 per cent annual indexation to 2029, intended to replace most negotiated CACs and density bonusing except for larger rezonings; ACC-funded programme about $483 million of a $7.7 billion 10-year capital programme; rental waivers; Northeast False Creek exempt. City CAC reporting: 2022 cash CACs $63M and density bonus zoning $29M (search snippet of City annual report; unconfirmed). The Bill 44 (2023) small-scale multi-unit housing framework came after Vancouver's R1-1 decision (Bill 44 third reading 29 Nov 2023; City complied for restricted zones in spring 2024; Bill 25 revisions in fall 2025) and is a provincial upzoning mandate, so it is a mistake to read the 2023 multiplex policy as a response to Bill 44.
content_summary.no_cmhc_statcan_claims: The essay contains no CMHC, StatCan or price data; no figures to anchor. Existing wiki objection page cites Wiebe's earlier essay for Vancouver prices ($400,000 in 2000 to over $3,000,000 'today'); that is a separate anchoring problem (see existing_wiki_coverage).

existing_wiki_coverage:
Wiebe: objections/planning-restrictions-cause-high-prices.md, Response point 4 and Source 7 cite his earlier post 'Do rising land values explain high housing prices?' (blog.michaelwiebe.com/p/do-rising-land-values-explain-high). The new essay is not cited anywhere. TIER 2 COMPLIANCE OF THE EXISTING CITATION: largely compliant. Good: introduced as 'Proponents further argue... The economics blogger Michael Wiebe makes the point', the quotations are framed as his conclusion, and Source 7 states 'Independent economics blog commentary, not peer-reviewed (D-claim)'; it is not in the lead; it is listed after Tier 1 sources. Points a Tier 1 editor should tidy: (a) it sits inside 'The Response' (an evidence section) rather than a labelled proponent section; §4c says Tier 2 names belong in a clearly labelled section, and the economic mechanism it states (rezoning capitalises a larger permitted use into land price) is already supported by Tier 1 items in the same list (Freemark 2020; Greenaway-McGrevy et al. 2021), so either relabel point 4 or substitute those and keep Wiebe as origin; (b) the Vancouver house-price figures ($400,000 in 2000 to over $3,000,000) are his unsourced numbers and should be dropped or replaced by an official series (Statistics Canada/CMHC/BC Assessment); (c) Source 7's wording 'article fetched and read 2026-08-14' is borderline process-narration under §4b rule 3; 'accessed 2026-08-14' is the impersonal form. His status: Substack bio 'economist interested in housing and replication'; his own site says PhD Economics, University of British Columbia, 2020, independent (reanalysis of empirical research, available for hire and as an expert witness in housing cases). The scanner's '(UBC)' is an alumnus link, not a current appointment. Consistent with people-tiers.json Tier 2. Note a queue item records a different 'Michael Wiebe' who is a Vancouver councillor; do not confuse.

Vancouver and BC coverage: places/vancouver.md and places/british-columbia.md cover only the 1910-1984 single-tax history, the Empty Homes Tax and the Speculation and Vacancy Tax; there is NO coverage of density bonus zoning, Community Amenity Contributions, the Cultural Amenity Bonus, Streamlining Rental, the R1-1 multiplex zone, Bill 44, Bill 46 or the 2026 ACC. concepts/land-value-capture.md lists instruments (betterment levies, TIF, leasing, LVIT, Ontario Community Benefit Charges, negotiated PILOTs) but not density bonusing, CACs or amenity cost charges; the word Vancouver does not appear there. research/cib-land-value-capture-study.md (Siemiatycki, Fagan & Arku 2023) defines density bonuses and cites Vancouver Capstan Station ($31.5M of a $52M station cost, 61 per cent, after nine years of negotiation; and one Vancouver mechanism that raised 'only $32 million'). research/dachis-buyers-beware-housing-barriers.md recommends land-value capture over per-unit development charges for Canadian cities and gives Vancouver's 2011-21 price-cost gap ($1.3M). research/nielsen-buitelaar-spatial-planning-anticipatory-rules.md (spatial planning as eliminating land rents) is a conceptually adjacent Tier 1 source. concepts/betterment-levy.md, problems/public-investment-capitalizes-into-land.md, concepts/residual-land-valuation.md, research/mcallister-developer-contributions-tpr.md and research/walters-property-taxes-value-capture-instruments.md are adjacent. No page for 'community amenity contribution' or 'density bonus' exists.
uncertainties: Both City documents the essay quotes are Cloudflare-blocked from this environment on every route tried, so the quoted phrases ('could impact land values significantly unless...'; 'would mitigate... thus absorbing any increases in land value') and the 600 / 2,600 sq ft figures are unverified. A Tier 1 editor on an unblocked network (or a human with a browser) should read them before any factual sentence is drafted from them.

Search-snippet items (City CAC annual-report totals, ACC adoption on 21 July 2026, 14 Sept 2023 hearing date, 3-6/8-unit rules) come from search-engine summaries of City pages and, for Shape Your City, from pages actually fetched. Items marked snippet-only should be confirmed from the City PDFs.

Vancouver ACC rate details come from a Daily Hive account of the staff report and the HAVAN trade summary; final by-law rates were not read. The by-law is expected at council.vancouver.ca/20260728/documents/Bylaws34to38.pdf (surfaced in search, not fetched).
Date of the VSO bonus (2005) rests on a single 2011 news article; the Council report was not located or read.

Whether Wiebe's reading (hostility to density) or the City's stated reading (limit land-price escalation and speculation so the policy remains viable) better explains the design is a matter of interpretation. The fee level is described by the City as feasibility-tested; the essay does not test its claim that a more permissive allowance would have raised more.
Wiebe's essay is one data point from a blogger who markets consulting/expert-witness services in housing cases; there is no peer-reviewed analysis behind it in this essay.
